But beyond the technical toolkit, I'm drawn to roles where quality is measured not just by whether something works, but by whether it remains comprehensible and modifiable as the product grows. That's the kind of environment where I work best: where a code review conversation is about keeping abstractions clean, where Jest coverage reflects genuine thoughtfulness rather than vanity metrics, and where a designer's intention isn't lost in translation to CSS and React components.

I'm interested in contributing to a team where frontend development is treated as a serious discipline rather than a series of technical choices. job_title: EngD in Human-AI Interaction for Sign Language Translation

motivation_letter.name: Goonja Gandhi
paragraphs: This EngD opportunity stands apart because it does not begin with a finished technology looking for a problem—it begins with users whose communication needs remain inadequately served by existing solutions. Sign language translation sits at the intersection of AI capability and human experience, where technical elegance means nothing if the interface does not reflect how Deaf and hard-of-hearing users actually interact with language. That alignment between rigorous user understanding and technical implementation is what draws me to this role.

My professional path has consistently moved toward understanding the layers beneath the interfaces I build. As a frontend engineer, I have spent five years delivering accessible, performant applications—but increasingly I have recognized that accessibility is not an afterthought or a compliance requirement; it is a fundamental design principle that reveals whether an interface truly serves its users. During my work at TCS, I enforced WCAG-compliant design practices across enterprise applications, achieving zero accessibility violations during QA. More recently, at Datapret, I led the design of a complaint resolution platform that increased WCAG compliance by 30%. That work taught me that building for accessibility requires thinking differently about how information is presented, how users navigate systems, and how interfaces fail when they assume a single mode of interaction.

What distinguishes this EngD from traditional frontend or AI engineering roles is that the technical challenge is inseparable from the user research challenge. Through my work with AI integrations, semantic search systems, and RAG pipelines in projects like NewsAlign, I have learned that AI systems fail not when their algorithms are weak, but when they do not account for how humans actually need to use them. Co-creation with Deaf and hard-of-hearing users, iterative evaluation of comprehensibility and naturalness, and translating lived experience into system requirements—these are not add-ons to engineering. They are the engineering. My background in accessibility, combined with hands-on experience building AI-mediated interfaces, positions me to contribute meaningfully to both the technical implementation and the user-centered evaluation that this role demands.

I understand that this position requires navigating the tension between academic rigor and practical iteration, between technical feasibility and user needs, between prototyping and evaluation. I am drawn to that complexity precisely because it resists simple solutions. The opportunity to work within an interdisciplinary team—another EngD, postdoc researchers, and partner organizations like BrainBite and Digitaal Toegankelijk—appeals to me because the most substantial problems in human-computer interaction require perspectives beyond engineering alone. Thank you for considering my application. I look forward to the opportunity to discuss how I can contribute.
